title: if, else, switch, and truthiness
hook: Curly braces { } define a block scope for let and const. Unlike C#, JavaScript if conditions accept any value — the engine coerces it to true or false using truthiness rules that trip up every developer coming from C# or Java.

sections.heading: What are if and switch statements?

blocks.text: A **statement** is a single instruction: assign a variable, call a function, or branch with if. A **block** is a group of statements inside `{ }` that share a scope for let/const. The **if statement** runs one branch when a condition is **truthy**. The **switch statement** compares an expression to case values using **strict equality (===)** — with optional fall-through unless you break. JavaScript has no required bool type in if — **truthiness** decides.

entries.plainDefinition: Any value that converts to true in a boolean context.
entries.example: Non-empty strings, non-zero numbers, objects, arrays, and functions are truthy.

entries.plainDefinition: One of eight values that convert to false: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN.
entries.example: if ("") does not run — empty string is falsy.

entries.plainDefinition: When a case matches and no break/return/throw exits, execution continues into the next case body.
entries.example: switch (n) { case 1: log(1); case 2: log(2); break; } logs twice for n === 1.

entries.plainDefinition: Statements grouped in { } creating scope for let/const and grouping else branches.
entries.example: if (ok) { const x = 1; } — x is not visible after the brace.

sections.heading: Why truthiness changes how you write guards

blocks.text: C# requires `if (count > 0)` — `if (count)` is a compile error. JavaScript allows `if (count)` which treats `0` as false. That is convenient for optional strings but dangerous for numeric APIs where zero is valid. Prefer **explicit comparisons** (`count > 0`, `name !== ""`, `value != null`) in production and interviews. Always use braces around if/else bodies — ASI and dangling else bugs are real.

blocks.title: Real-world auth branching
blocks.body: Use if/else chains when the discriminator is a small set of strings (issuer, role). Use switch when many constant cases need a dispatch-table shape — remember break or return each case. For optional config, `if (config?.enabled)` relies on truthiness of the boolean property, not the object.

sections.heading: How if and switch execute step by step

items.title: Evaluate the condition expression
items.body: Any type is allowed — not just boolean.

items.title: Apply ToBoolean
items.body: The engine converts the value to true or false using truthiness rules.

items.title: Enter the matching branch
items.body: Run the if block when truthy, else if chain, or else.

items.title: Exit block scope
items.body: let/const bindings inside { } end at the closing brace.

diagram.source:
flowchart TD

  B -->|case lti| C[Run lti body]
  B -->|case local| D[Run local body]
  B -->|no match| E[default body]
  C --> F{break / return / throw?}
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F -->|no break| G[Fall through to next case]
  F -->|break| H[Exit switch]

snippet.label: Truthy and falsy in if conditions
snippet.explanation: Only eight values are falsy. Empty arrays and objects are truthy — a common interview trick question.

snippet.label: if/else chain for token issuer
snippet.explanation: Explicit string compare avoids truthiness surprises. Same pattern as C# but without required bool in the condition when you use comparisons.

snippet.label: switch with === and intentional fall-through
snippet.explanation: Stacked cases share one body without executing intermediate code — unlike C# goto case. Missing break after case 500 falls into 502.

snippet.label: Nullish check vs truthiness
snippet.explanation: == null catches both null and undefined by design — one of the few justified == uses. Prefer explicit checks in hot paths.

blocks.title: Truthiness traps
blocks.body: if (value) when 0 or "" are valid. if ([]) assuming empty means false. switch without break causing accidental fall-through. switch (x) where x is an object — cases compare by === reference, not deep equality. Dangling else when omitting braces near nested ifs.

blocks.title: Eight falsy values — memorize for interviews
blocks.body: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy — including [], {}, and "false".

interviewTakeaways: if accepts any value; engine applies ToBoolean — not C# bool-only rules.
Falsy list: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN — everything else truthy.
switch uses ===; break prevents fall-through; stacked cases are idiomatic.
60s: C# if needs bool; JS uses truthiness. Empty array is truthy. Prefer explicit compares for numbers and strings. switch === not deep equal.
Follow-up: why is typeof null === "object" and how does that affect if (obj) checks?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'Empty array is falsy' — [] is truthy; only "" among common empties is falsy.
Weak: 'switch compares values like deepEqual' — strict reference/value === only.
Strong: 'Explicit guards for numbers and strings. Memorize eight falsies. break every switch case unless fall-through is documented.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# if (count) fails compile — must write count > 0. Biggest mindset shift for C# devs learning JS truthiness.
TypeScript @typescript-eslint/strict-boolean-expressions flags if (str) when str is string | null. Narrows types better with explicit checks.
